edges.relationship: Winter’s study of Great War mourning connects memory research to war’s cultural aftermath
edges.evidence_note: Remembrance becomes an object of historical inquiry; not all military history is memory studies. The checked introduction questions a clean modernist rupture and explicitly limits transfer to later catastrophes. This specifies a contribution to military/war history without identifying it with operational history.
edges.map_label: Winter: mourning after the Great War

edges.relationship: Tony Judt: The Age of Extremes keeps the categories of the 1930s, gives Bolshevism “no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms”, devotes “just six pages” to “real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia and neglects nationalism (1995)
edges.evidence_note: A named reader without a node, drawn from political history because his charge concerns the book's political history. Judt (NYRB, 25 May 1995, read in full): the book's "defect, for there is really only one" is that "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; the claim that Sovietisation followed American intervention "is simply wrong"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject"; Hobsbawm "mostly avoids military or political narrative". Qualifications kept: Judt calls the book "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account", praises its economic analysis and calls The Age of Capital "Hobsbawm’s single greatest work". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.
edges.map_label: Judt on The Age of Extremes, 1995

edges.relationship: Cronon builds on White’s distinction between chronicle and narrative, then sides with David Carr against the White–Mink view that historians impose plots on reality (1992)
edges.evidence_note: Cronon's own text, read in part for this edge ("A Place for Stories", JAH 78:4, 1992, author-hosted copy in journal pagination): p. 1351 n. 7, "This distinction between chronicle and narrative is more fully analyzed in White, Metahistory, 5-7; White, Tropics of Discourse, 109-11"; p. 1368, White and Mink "argue that narrative is so basic to our cultural beliefs that we automatically impose it on a reality that bears little or no relation to the plots we use" (Cronon's summary of their position); n. 39 calls White's 1984 survey "useful, if biased"; pp. 1368–1369, Carr's position "gives us a way of absorbing the lessons of narrative theory without feeling we have abandoned all ties to an external reality". One essay makes both moves, so one arrow records an acknowledged and contested resource (the pattern of edge_646). edge_903 (Cronon → truthdebate) uses other pages of the same essay for his own position.
edges.map_label: Chronicle and narrative: used and contested, 1992

edges.relationship: Tilly: 'shrill bravado', 'softcore solipsism' and a dismissal of democratic politics that his own evidence contradicts (1994); Lawrence asked 'The Decline of English Popular Politics?' (1994); Oddy found 'verbose but superficial' method in Hunger (2008); Craig doubted modernity as a singular condition (2016)
edges.evidence_note: Tilly 1994, read in full: 'Joyce fretfully and Vernon with shrill bravado' (p. 260); 'the Joyce-Vernon philosophical position obliterates any possibility of historical explanation' (p. 261); by Tilly's criteria Vernon's own evidence 'establishes a modest but real increase in democracy' (p. 268). Oddy (Reviews in History 695, read in full): 'the lack of methodological rigour which is evident in his verbose but superficial style'; Vernon's response read. Craig (2016, read) doubts modernity as a singular condition. Lawrence's 1994 review is known by its title only. Vernon's own answers are on his entry and on his 2009 response to Oddy.

edges.relationship: Named answers: Cannadine, in Joyce's report of the unread review, asked for 'a history of status' and in reply caricatured Joyce's populism (1992–93); Tilly found 'softcore solipsism' and 'a doubt sandwich' (1994); Kirk 'a materialist view' (1994); Eley and Nield, in Joyce's report, equated his questioning of social history 'with contemporary neo-liberalism' (1995); Koditschek a 'class-evacuated analytical approach' (2014)
edges.evidence_note: The December 1992 review is unread; Joyce's letter (NYRB, 8 April 1993, read) reports that it ended by calling for 'a history of status' rather than 'a history of class' or 'a history of language', and answers that the categories of populism 'are important precisely for their plasticity not despite it' and open 'a history of social unities' that 'will at once be a history of difference'. Cannadine's reply (read) calls the letter 'disappointingly predictable' and caricatures Joyce's position — status 'merely a "rhetorical construction"', class 'rejected because it is a "grand concept"' — as Cannadine's summary of Joyce, not his own view of status or class. Tilly (1994, read in full): 'Joyce tortures himself on a rack of his own manufacture'; 'a doubt sandwich: a hearty slab of old-fashioned research between two layers of uncertainty' (pp. 263–265). Kirk 1994 by title only. Eley and Nield's 'Starting Over' (1995) is unread; the 'neo-liberalism' charge is Joyce's characterisation (1996, p. 96, read), as is their 'denial of creative conversations'; their 2000 essay (read) finds Democratic Subjects 'with no moorings to the densely contextualized studies of working-class life social historians have come to require' (p. 6). Koditschek (JBS 2014, read): 'class-evacuated analytical approach'; still 'Joyce's best, most innovative, and most insightful book—so far'. Mayfield and Thorne's 1993 reply to his note: metadata only. Joyce's own answers are on his entry.

edges.relationship: Visions of the People (1991) against the chronology of class fixed by Thompson and Hobsbawm: 'the fixation with class' denied sight of 'other visions of the social order'; 'because manual workers chose to wear cloth caps and support football teams, it does not follow that they saw the social order in terms of class' (p. 8, as quoted by Tilly)
edges.evidence_note: Own words: introduction p. 1 (chapter opening read): 'while there is no denying that class was a child of the nineteenth century, when it comes to how the social order was represented and understood, there were other children too who were every bit as lusty as class'; p. 8 as quoted by Tilly (1994, p. 264, read in full), against Hobsbawm; ch. 14 opening (p. 329): 'rather than a single populism, it is a variety or "family" of populisms that should be considered'; 'The controlling narrative of popular politics appears to have concerned a righteous and dispossessed "people" rather than a "working class"'. Tilly's judgement that 'by most standards he has also documented the salience of working-class identities' (p. 265) is the counterweight. The book's body is unread.

edges.relationship: Thompson's Making 'presents a picture of class consciousness as substantially "made" by around 1830'; this 'received wisdom has in fact become a dead weight' (1991). Tilly answered that Joyce and Vernon 'remain captives of Thompson' and 'engage in Thompsonian hermeneutics' (1994)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, introduction p. 1 (chapter opening read): 'the work of E. P. Thompson and E. J. Hobsbawm remained, and remains, central, fixing the historical sequence of class development … Received wisdom has in fact become a dead weight, the fixation with class denying us sight of these other visions of the social order.' Tilly 1994, pp. 262–263 (read in full): 'Joyce and Vernon nevertheless remain captives of Thompson … They engage in Thompsonian hermeneutics'; 'it was Thompson above all who argued that class was not an individual state of mind … but a dynamic, contested relationship among sets of people'. Hobsbawm is named in the same sentence; no separate arrow is drawn to him.

edges.relationship: A settler-colonial analytic worked out in conversation with Native American and Indigenous Studies: US Indian policy (removal, allotment, blood quantum, termination) read as successive modalities of elimination (2006, 2011); 'a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking' (Goeman, 2016)
edges.evidence_note: Goeman 2016 (read in full): "a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking and scholarship that exists far longer than settler nations"; "He critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner". Kauanui 2016 (read in full), note 7: "his long time, direct intellectual engagement with scholars in Native American and Indigenous Studies", and para. 2: he insisted "that Native scholars did" create the field. Wolfe 2006 (read in full), sections on discovery and preemption, the Cherokee removal, allotment, blood quantum ("statistical extermination", quoting Jaimes) and termination; "After the Frontier" (2011) is unread. A contribution to the conversation, not an origin: the entry's Indigenous methods are not derived from him, and the dissent of Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014) is recorded on the entry. Replaces the former comparison row. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: Race as the outcome of 'differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process' (2001): 'a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting'; Black people 'racialized as slaves', Indians eliminated 'as Indians' (2006); a comparative typology of colonial race regimes in Traces of History (2016)
edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), opening section: "different racial regimes encode and reproduce the unequal relationships into which Europeans coerced the populations concerned"; "Black people's enslavement produced an inclusive taxonomy … For Indians, in stark contrast, non-Indian ancestry compromised their indigeneity"; "a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting"; and note 62 quoting his own 2001 essay, p. 894: "Difference … is not simply given. It is the outcome of differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process." The 2001 essay is otherwise unread (Crossref: AHR 106:3, June 2001). Traces of History (2016) known through the British Library contents note (chapters on Australia, the United States, central Europe, Brazil, Palestine) and Veracini's obituary (read): it "utilises his analysis of racism under settler colonialism in order to explain racism everywhere else" and provides "a compelling typology of racial formations". Strengthens the entry-level comparison edge_885, which stays. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: Interprets Reconstruction through Black political action, contested freedom and the struggle to build democracy.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview answers stress change after slavery and oppose treating later injustice as proof that emancipation changed nothing.

edges.relationship: Traces competing meanings of freedom rather than treating freedom as one stable national possession.
edges.evidence_note: In the interview Foner explicitly contrasts economic equality and rights with narrow anti-government definitions, and rejects narratives that absorb every struggle into a stable Americanism.

edges.relationship: Critically reworks the economic-conflict interpretation and explores ideological consensus in American politics.
edges.evidence_note: Foner distinguishes Hofstadter’s critical consensus interpretation from celebratory versions and notes the later reconsideration of conflict.

edges.relationship: Brings status anxiety, symbols and irrationality into accounts of political culture.
edges.evidence_note: Foner’s named substantive reading also judges the treatment of Populists and Progressives exaggerated and elitist in important respects. This qualification survives the contribution arrow.

edges.relationship: Cohen’s move from workers and consumers to a powerful planner retains social history’s attention to class, gender, race and ethnicity.
edges.evidence_note: Own BackStory answer on research design explicitly identifies the continuity and change; no assertion that biography replaces social history.

edges.relationship: Interprets enslaved culture and paternalism as contested forms within a system of domination.
edges.evidence_note: Existing complete preface and initial paternalism paragraphs, plus Walter Johnson’s complete retrospective, within their recorded scopes. Paternalism is not a benign-slavery claim; Johnson’s consent/coercion criticism remains visible.

edges.relationship: Makes the relation between slaveholding class power, economic organization and development a problem for Marxist historical interpretation.
edges.evidence_note: Specific political-economy intervention mediated by N. Gordon Levin’s substantive review, selected opening pages. This is a contribution to a contested interpretation, not proof that every Marxist shared it, or a direct personal influence from Marx or Gramsci.

edges.relationship: Challenges a categorical boundary between Indigenous life and modernity through the case of Mary Sully’s art.
edges.evidence_note: Primary written answer on being native to modernism, 2024. The argument concerns a distinctive artist and does not make her representative of all Indigenous people. The complete book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Explains a collaborative route from family-held drawings through historical research and public talks to museum interpretation.
edges.evidence_note: Primary Q&A answers on rediscovery, curatorial challenges, book formation and exhibitions. Deloria credits his mother, audiences and named curators; this records historical/public interpretation, not sole creation of the art or a generic museum affiliation.

edges.relationship: Explains American political development through western settlement and changing social forces.
edges.evidence_note: Primary frontier opening and 1910 address ground the interpretation; “free land” is a settler premise that obscures Indigenous sovereignty.

edges.relationship: Calls for combined economic, political, geographic and social inquiry rather than isolated specialist explanations.
edges.evidence_note: Read 1910 address explicitly argues that human social factors are varied and complex; no claim Turner founded later comparative historical sociology.

edges.relationship: Taylor’s continental frame links national conflicts through cross-border intervention and political interdependence.
edges.evidence_note: Own2024 interview on Mexican civil wars, Canadian confederation and American secession; continental linkage, not an exhaustive world history.

edges.relationship: Taylor compares rival projects of union, liberal rights and sovereignty across North American polities.
edges.evidence_note: Own2024 answers on Lincoln/Juárez and threats to union; describes a substantive political-history contribution without treating liberal ideals as universal outcomes.

edges.relationship: Noiriel’s socio-history connects archival reconstruction to relationships of power and social interdependence.
edges.evidence_note: Own2012 opening describes a collective project influenced by sociology,not a claim of sole foundation or institutional membership.

edges.relationship: Reinterprets Prohibition as consequential state-building and political realignment.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview describes expanded enforcement while expressly denying it alone caused the later carceral state.

edges.relationship: Gerstle’s political-order concept explains durable settlements whose assumptions constrain governing parties and their opponents.
edges.evidence_note: Own2022 opening definition and New Deal/neoliberal comparison; historical model rather than a fixed law or inevitable sequence.

edges.relationship: Gramscian resources enter distinct Genovese and Gutman interpretations
edges.evidence_note: One disputed application within a heterogeneous radical historiography, not the origin of the US New Left. Gutman pp. 584–585 explicitly quotes Gramsci through Tilly on elite perceptions of subordinate groups. Genovese’s hegemony application is supported here by Johnson’s retrospective account; a direct original Gramsci passage in Genovese remains unread. These are different mechanisms and evidence scopes.

edges.relationship: De Vries uses demographic research on marriage, mortality, fertility and households to revise accounts of early modern economic change
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. His 1994 article, p. 252, explicitly discusses demographic contributions and cites Henry, Laslett, Hajnal, Wrigley and Schofield among others. This named use strengthens the formerly generic field link. Hajnal’s own primary argument is now checked separately: it includes category/geography limits and economic hypotheses in both causal directions. De Vries’s particular use does not convert these into a proved general mechanism.
edges.map_label: De Vries: demographic patterns complicate growth histories

edges.relationship: Curtin’s census contributes quantitative reconstruction of the slave trade
edges.evidence_note: Curtin’s book replaces Gilroy as the reference. Its estimates were subsequently revised; quantitative inquiry did not begin or end with this book. The current Curtin check is bibliographic; numerical series and the later 1999 database still require separate review.

edges.relationship: De Vries links expanding demand with household labor and resource reallocation
edges.evidence_note: The 1994 article provides a named demand-and-labor intervention in explanations of industrialization, while qualifying household unity and universal stages. It does not make consumption history the sole source of the argument.
edges.map_label: De Vries: demand and the industrious revolution

edges.relationship: Benson explicitly challenges the economic-determinist interpretation he attributes to Turner and Beard
edges.evidence_note: Chapter VIII opening names both historians. The target is the Progressive side of the paired entry and a specified interpretation; it is not criticism of every argument by them or every consensus historian.
edges.map_label: Benson: criticism of economic-determinist voting history

edges.relationship: Cannadine questions the causal argument and uneven treatment of power in Queen Victoria
edges.evidence_note: This group arrow identifies Cannadine’s 1990 review specifically. It records disagreement over connections to women’s rights and republicanism, not unanimous judgment or endorsement of the reviewer’s incidental biographical claims.

edges.relationship: Wallerstein contests Dobb’s definition of capitalism and the transitional period
edges.evidence_note: Wallerstein 1974 pp. 393, 399 names Dobb and quotes Capitalism Yesterday and Today. He prefers a world-economy/market-production unit that includes coerced labor. This records disagreement, not a verdict against Dobb’s historical evidence.
edges.map_label: Wallerstein challenges Dobb’s unit and definition

edges.relationship: Settler colonialism as 'a structure not an event': settler colonizers 'come to stay'; the form 'destroys to replace', is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal', has territory as its 'irreducible element' and persists after the frontier as 'structural genocide' (1994–2006)
edges.evidence_note: Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_01): the 2006 essay, read in full in the Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page (screq_wolfe_2006 addendum), joins the 1999 introduction (pp. 1–2, read earlier: settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies'; 'invasion is a structure not an event'; contents and catalogue checked). Wolfe 2006, in his words: 'Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal' (p. 387, pages per Kauanui 2016); 'Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event' (p. 388; his note 7 refers the formula to the 1999 book, p. 2, and to 'Nation and MiscegeNation', 1994, p. 96); 'Settler colonialism destroys to replace'; 'elimination refers to more than the summary liquidation of Indigenous people, though it includes that' (p. 390); 'settler colonialism is relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' (p. 403). A contribution, not a founding: earlier settler-society studies (1983, 1995) and earlier usage (Veracini 2013; Kauanui 2016, note 7: Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973) precede it, and Kauanui records that Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did'. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note (user rule, 2026-10-23); bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: A history of Victorian and Australian anthropology in its settler-colonial setting
edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1999). The contents page lists chapters on mother-right ('Sex and Property in Victorian Anthropology'), totemism ('Victorian Anthropology's Eternal Dichotomy') and E. B. Tylor ('Survival in a Paradigm Shift: E.B. Tylor and the Problem of the Text'), alongside virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse. Catalogue subjects: Anthropology -- Australia -- History; Racism in anthropology -- Australia. Introduction p. 1 read: the book is 'a history not so much of anthropology itself as of its ideological entanglements'. The chapters' stance toward these anthropologists is not read here. If the introduction confirms a critical argument, a critique edge to anthropology/evolution may be the better reading. A historian's account of the discipline, not anthropological fieldwork. Addendum 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_02): Veracini's obituary (read in full) reports that the 1999 book 'was ostensibly a history of Australian anthropology', that 'settler colonialism' was 'only added at the very end and at the request of the publisher', and that 'to explain the evolution of anthropology Patrick defined settler colonialism as distinct from colonialism'; Goeman (read in full) records Audra Simpson's memory of him as a historian 'of anthropology itself, and its relationship to politics'. The chapters remain unread, so the critique/contribution question stays open.

edges.relationship: Narrative bounded by evidence, ecology and the community of scholars: an environmental historian’s answer to postmodern critiques of narrative (1992); twenty years on, 'Storytelling' (2013) restated the case: 'How do we make the past come alive? By telling stories about it', referring readers to the 1992 essay for 'this theoretical background'
edges.evidence_note: 'A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative', JAH 78:4 (March 1992), author-hosted copy in journal pagination (pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read). Writing about narrative, 'we cannot avoid encountering the postmodernist assault on narrative, which calls into question not just the stories we tell but the deeper purpose that motivated us in the first place' (p. 1349). The argument is meant for all historians: 'I am urging historians to acknowledge storytelling as the necessary core even of longue durée histories … Environmental history is but one example of these, and most of my arguments apply just as readily to the others' (p. 1349, n. 5). 'I, like most practicing historians, am only willing to follow the postmodernists so far'; 'My goal throughout has been to acknowledge the immense power of narrative while still defending the past (and nature) as real things to which our storytelling must somehow conform lest it cease being history altogether' (p. 1372). Three bounds: 'our stories cannot contravene known facts about the past' and 'our stories must make ecological sense' (p. 1372); 'We write as members of communities' (p. 1373). 'To just that extent, nature coauthors our stories' (p. 1373). Against 'an endless postmodernist deconstruction of texts that fails to ground itself in history, in community, in politics, and finally in the moral problem of living on earth' he asserts 'the virtues of narrative' (p. 1374), and he asks environmental historians for 'not just stories about nature, but stories about stories about nature' (p. 1375). He reads with Hayden White’s Metahistory, Tropics of Discourse and The Content of the Form and with Novick (nn. 6, 7, 43), and credits Richard White with the argument about criticism (n. 46). The 1993 address restates it: historical wisdom 'usually comes in the form of parables, not policy recommendations or certainties' (p. 16). This is his own text; no in-period reading that places the essay in the postmodernism debate was read. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_903 revision): the 2013 address read in passages (AHA open text; n. 14 refers to 'A Place for Stories').

edges.relationship: The middle ground: accommodation through mutual invention and creative misunderstanding between Algonquian villages and empires in the Great Lakes region, 1650–1815 (1991)
edges.evidence_note: White's own statement, The Middle Ground (1991). Introduction, p. ix (Cambridge Core first-page excerpt: the full page, folio observed): histories of Indian–white relations have had 'but two outcomes', stories 'of conquest and assimilation' or 'of cultural persistence'; their tellers 'miss a larger process and a larger truth. The meeting of sea and continent, like the meeting of whites and Indians, creates as well as destroys.' The next page (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi; witnessed only by Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition, page images not seen, the 1991 page inferred) defines the middle ground, in paraphrase, as the space between cultures, between peoples, and between empires and the stateless world of villages, where differences were accommodated through creative and often expedient misunderstanding, and explains it by the long periods in which whites could neither command Indians nor ignore them. Chapter 2 opening (p. 50, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt, folio observed): French and Algonquians 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting; they had to create what I have already referred to as a middle ground. The creation of the middle ground involved a process of mutual invention by both the French and the Algonquians.' It rested on 'the need of people to find a means, other than force, to gain the cooperation or consent of foreigners' (p. 52), and was, in paraphrase, a product both of everyday life and of formal diplomacy between distinct peoples (p. 53) (both Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition; page numbers as the snippet results give them, taken to match 1991). Chapter 3 opening (p. 94, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): the fur trade was 'a constantly changing compromise, a conduit, between two local models of the exchange'. Epilogue (p. 518, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): 'The compromises intrinsic in the middle ground yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness.' In-period reception, each read in full. Savard (1992; Université de Montréal anthropologist) judges the book's circularity 'inattaquable' and suited to 'bien d'autres époques et régions de l'Amérique du Nord', but asks whether the Algonquians' shattered prior state and Iroquois military supremacy, 'cet autre mythe fondateur de la république américaine', were needed to explain it (p. 120). Edmunds (1993) calls the thesis 'a valuable model for the exploration of the Indian-French relationship' (p. 148) and the book possibly 'a landmark volume in the ethnohistory of the Great Lakes tribes', but finds 'his arguments for the period after 1770 are less convincing' (p. 149). D. R. Miller (1994, Canadian Journal of Native Studies, from the Saskatchewan Indian Federated College) calls it 'an extraordinary benchmark in the scholarship of European and Aboriginal relations' (p. 157), notes that White 'deemphasizes the specificity of a small number of groups in the larger Great Lakes region that are neither Iroquoian or Algonquian' (p. 158), and writes that 'The challenge for a similar study with emphasis upon the north side of the Great Lakes is obvious' (p. 170). The edge records a scholar's interpretation of Indigenous–imperial relations, which the Indigenous history entry lists as related scholarship; it does not make the work an Indigenous historical practice or a source of Indigenous authority. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: White's 2011 preface (Google Books search-within snippets only) answers Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999; cited pp. xx–xxi) and the later critiques of Havard (Empire et métissages, 2003; p. xvi) and Deloria ('What Is the Middle Ground, Anyway?', 2006; cited p. xii; both unread here): the middle ground 'did not involve the achievement of a widespread mutual understanding and appreciation between Europeans and Indian peoples. People did not come together to love one another' (p. xxi), and he did not think that 'every time you find this process at work you would find the construction of a coherent space that is the equivalent of pays d'en haut' (p. xiii). McNeill (2003; text-layer PDF) reports that the concept 'struck historians of Japan and medieval Austria as useful for their own studies' (p. 37).

edges.relationship: Environmental change through land use, subsistence and labour: Island County (1980), the roots of Native dependency (1983) and the Columbia as an organic machine (1995), with an early survey of the field (1985)
edges.evidence_note: White's own statements, known for his books only through Google Books search-within snippets (page images not seen) and therefore paraphrased where the wording carries the claim. Land Use, Environment, and Social Change (1980; snippets of the 1992 paperback, whose body text is the 1980 text; p. 7 as given in the snippet results): White presents the book as departing somewhat from recent environmental history, which he describes as mostly a variant of intellectual and political history, by tracing the environmental impact of Indian and later intruding peoples and its consequences for their societies; on the same page he credits James Malin's Great Plains studies, ignored by most historians, as a trail to follow. In the preface to the 1992 edition (November 1991; snippet, folio xviii inferred from Google Books page ids that carry the printed folios xi, xvi and xvii) he judges his own use of ecology: 'I used ecological concepts like community, succession, climax, and ecosystem unproblematically even though within the discipline of ecology those ideas had already come under attack'. Cronon's foreword (October 1991; snippets, folio xi observed) places the book among White's contributions 'to environmental history, to the history of the American West, to Indian history, and to American history generally' and calls it 'a textbook case of an underappreciated classic' (p. xi). The Organic Machine (1995; snippets of the preface, whose printed folios were not visible, and of the conclusion, p. 112 taken from the Google Books page id, not seen as a printed folio), in paraphrase: White examines the Columbia as an organic machine, an energy system modified by human intervention that keeps natural, unmade qualities; human labour is energy as much as the river's flow or the calories salmon store for their journey; environmentalists, he argues, distance humans from nature by favouring the eye over the hand and contemplation over work; and the conclusion finds the nature in us in our labour and energy (p. 112). In-period third-party readings: Cronon (1993; OCR of the author-hosted page scan) footnotes Land Use and The Roots of Dependency (nn. 15, 23) for the lesson that 'the horse was not simply a European invader, but a complex cultural entity' (p. 9); D. R. Miller (1994; PDF read in full) calls him 'The social and environmental historian Richard White' (p. 157) and quotes The Middle Ground that dependency 'is an economic, political, and social relationship, but can also be an environmental relationship' (p. 169). On the 1985 survey (unread; paywalled): Worster (1990, read in the 2002–03 Portuguese translation, n. 5, p. 42) calls it the best effort to trace the field's emergence, 'pelo menos em uma parte influente do mundo', reporting White's view that frontier and western history was the formative influence; Cronon's 1994 graduate syllabus assigns it 'read for main themes' (p. 4); in Canada, Cook (1990) cites it (n. 4) for Turner and Webb as 'important, if declining, influences into the 1950s' (p. 6). A contribution, not a founding. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013) names White among historians who 'synthesized the material and cultural approaches to the environment' (p. 87) and quotes his 1990 round-table objection that Worster's scheme reduced culture to 'superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense' (pp. 88–89, citing JAH 76, pp. 1112–1113; the JAH text is unread).
edges.map_label: Land use, labour and the field, 1980–1995

edges.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, and the frontierism Canadian historians took from it, criticised as environmental determinism; the frontier recast as a dependent of the metropolis (1954)
edges.evidence_note: His own words. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History' (1954), read in full. He summarises Turner's thesis that 'the greatest formative influence' in American history had been 'the open frontier, the hither edge of free land' (p. 6) and judges: 'This was environmental determinism at its most forthright. The wilderness and the men it produced had made America' (p. 7). Against it he sets the metropolitan reading: the frontier's culture 'originally stems from a metropolitan community; at root, learning and ideas radiate from there—and thus is Turner answered' (p. 18); 'the frontier, far from being essentially independent and self-reliant, is in the largest sense a dependent' (p. 18); and 'the functioning of metropolitanism may do more to explain the course of Canadian history than concepts of frontierism borrowed from the United States and set forth before the significance of the modern metropolis was clear' (p. 20). 'At any rate, frontierism, along with earlier schools and approaches, has had its use and its day' (p. 21). His qualifications are kept: 'Defenders of Turner might claim that he had not proposed a frontier hypothesis as the only key to American history' (p. 7); the frontier thesis 'proper' was never 'adopted as fully or dogmatically in Canada as it was in the United States—and there, of course, it has long been the subject of qualification and criticism' (p. 1); Canadian environmentalists took over 'the general approach and mood of Turner and company ... rather than the precise frontier thesis, which received little direct application in Canada' (p. 6). He draws on American critics of Turner (Hayes, Fox, Schlesinger Jr.; pp. 7–8) and on Canadian ones (McDougall 1929, Stanley 1940; p. 10, n. 21). The critique is therefore aimed at Turner's thesis and above all at its Canadian adaptation; the Canadian historians he names sit in cdn_national_tradition and are covered by edge 1. In-period reading: Davis (1985, p. 95, read) calls the article 'Conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner'. Davis (p. 109) also quotes Careless on television saying of Turner's thesis that 'like any view of history which gets oversimplified, overpopularized, it becomes untrue; it becomes a myth' (undated, a quoted-in witness). No reply by a Turnerian historian was found or read.

edges.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, as taken up by Canadian historians in the 1930s and 1940s, rejected as an imported 'continental revelation' that Canadian history would not fit (1957)
edges.evidence_note: His own text, the 1957 CHA presidential address (read in full). Canadian historians had 'accepted, for historical purposes, the two highly fashionable political theories which dominated the thought of the inter-war and war years': 'the Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'the Frontier Theory' (p. 6). Of the second: 'Turner ... fixed upon the movement of settlement across the continent as the most important fact in its history'; 'the source of creative inspiration and action was found not at the centre, but at the periphery, of western culture' (p. 8). Applied to Canada, 'painful difficulties were immediately encountered': the frontier's progress 'had been evidently modified by all sorts of extraneous and unnatural things such as railways, efficient police, governmental supervision'; in 1837 'the rebels had come, not from the frontier, but from the older settled parts of the province'; yet its believers 'kept insisting that Canadian democracy was "forest-born"' (p. 9). He ends: historians bought 'a couple of suits of imported intellectual reach-me-downs' and a new generation would show 'less deference for imported theories of historical change and more respect for the manifold facts of Canadian experience' (p. 12). The critique inverts his own Laurentian premise, that change radiates from the centre. Limits: the address is a polemic and names no Canadian frontierist; Turner is not quoted beyond the phrases Creighton cites, and the atlas's own reading of Turner (progressive/multiple_hypotheses) shows him advocating multiple hypotheses rather than a single doctrine. Context: Careless's 1954 CHR article, unread here, was 'conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner' (Davis 1985, p. 95). No in-period reply to the address was looked for.
